title: Sentinel Automation, Retention, and Purview Audit

questions.sub_skill: Implement automation rules and playbooks in Microsoft Sentinel
questions.prompt: An automation rule is configured to run a playbook on incident creation. Incidents are created, the playbook never runs, and the rule reports no error. Most likely cause?
options: The playbook's trigger type is incident rather than alert
Sentinel lacks the Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor role on the playbook's resource group
The playbook's managed identity lacks Responder on the workspace
The automation rule's order places it after a closing rule
questions.explanation: This is the silent failure the role exists to prevent — the rule looks correct and does nothing, with no error where you would look for one. It is also the reason Automation Contributor is assigned to the Sentinel service rather than to a person.
why_not: An incident trigger is the right one for a rule that fires on incident creation.
Launching the playbook is not the playbook identity's job. Sentinel itself needs Automation Contributor on the playbook's resource group.
Nothing in the scenario involves another rule. A playbook that never runs, with no error, is the permissions gap this role exists to prevent.
questions.scenario_clue: "the playbook never runs" and "no error" - Sentinel lacks permission on the playbook's resource group.
questions.misconception: That a playbook's own identity is what lets Sentinel launch it.

questions.sub_skill: Implement automation rules and playbooks in Microsoft Sentinel
questions.prompt: Name one task only an automation rule can do, and one only a playbook can do.
options: Only a rule can add a comment; only a playbook can change severity
Only a rule can suppress incidents with an expiration date; only a playbook can reach an external system such as a ticketing tool
Only a rule can call an external API; only a playbook can assign an owner
Only a rule can run on a schedule; only a playbook can close an incident
questions.explanation: Automation rules are the routing layer — trigger, conditions, order, status and severity changes, suppression with an expiry. Playbooks are the action layer and can reach anything Logic Apps can reach.
why_not: Both can add comments, and changing severity is something automation rules do.
It is the reverse: reaching an external API is what playbooks are for, and assigning an owner is available to automation rules.
Automation rules run on incident and alert events, not on a schedule, and closing an incident is a status change they can make.
questions.scenario_clue: "only an automation rule" versus "only a playbook" - routing versus reaching external systems.
questions.misconception: That automation rules and playbooks are interchangeable.

questions.sub_skill: Implement data retention in Microsoft Sentinel data stores
questions.prompt: A table has 90 days of analytics retention and two years of total retention, with the older data in the data lake tier. An investigation needs data from 14 months ago. What do you do?
options: Query it with an analytics rule - total retention means it is available to rules
Run a search job or a KQL job against the data lake (or notebook), which returns the results you need; it takes time and carries its own charges
Re-ingest the data from the original source
Raise analytics retention to 24 months, which brings back data that has already left the analytics tier
questions.explanation: Data beyond analytics retention is kept, but it is not available to analytics rules or interactive hunting. Reach it with a search job, KQL job or notebook (or restore, for long-term retention). "We have two years of data" and "we can query two years of data" are different claims with different price tags.
why_not: Data in the data lake tier is not available to analytics rules or interactive hunting.
Re-ingesting duplicates data you already retain, at ingestion cost. Jobs against the lake exist for exactly this.
Raising analytics retention changes how long new and still-present data stays in the analytics tier; it is not how you query data already in the lake.
questions.scenario_clue: "14 months ago" with "90 days of analytics retention" - the data is in the lake, so you need a job, not a rule.
questions.misconception: That data you retain is data you can query the same way as recent data.

questions.sub_skill: Query Microsoft Purview Audit in Defender XDR
questions.prompt: During a mailbox compromise investigation you can list the messages the attacker accessed, but you also need to know what they searched for inside the mailbox. What determines whether that is possible?
options: Whether Sentinel's OfficeActivity connector was enabled
Whether the user held an Audit (Premium) licence with the Advanced Auditing service plan, because SearchQueryInitiated is an Audit (Premium) insight
Whether MailItemsAccessed was enabled for the mailbox
Whether the mailbox was placed on litigation hold
questions.explanation: MailItemsAccessed (part of Audit Standard mailbox auditing for E3/E5 users) tells you which messages were accessed. SearchQueryInitiated - what the attacker searched for in Exchange or SharePoint - is an Audit (Premium) intelligent insight, generated only for users with the licence and the Advanced Auditing service plan. That decision was made months before the incident.
why_not: The OfficeActivity connector brings audit records into Sentinel. It cannot create a SearchQueryInitiated record that was never generated.
MailItemsAccessed already answered the first question. Search activity is a separate, Audit (Premium) event.
Litigation hold preserves mailbox content. It does not record searches.
questions.scenario_clue: "what they searched for inside the mailbox" - SearchQueryInitiated, an Audit (Premium) insight.
questions.misconception: That every mailbox audit event comes with the base audit licence.

questions.sub_skill: Query Microsoft Purview Audit in Defender XDR
questions.prompt: Audit search returns nothing at all, for every query, across every workload. What do you check first?
options: The audit retention policy, which may have expired the records
Whether unified audit log ingestion is enabled — it can be turned off tenant-wide, and an attacker who does so has blinded the whole organisation
Whether your account holds the Audit Reader role
Whether the Defender portal has finished indexing
questions.explanation: Get-AdminAuditLogConfig reports UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled. Nothing across everything is a very different symptom from nothing for one workload, and in a real tenant a disabled audit log is a finding in its own right.
why_not: Expired records would leave gaps in older data, not silence for every query across every workload.
Silence across everything points at ingestion being off tenant-wide. That is the check that explains every workload at once.
An indexing delay affects recent events, not every query across every workload.
questions.scenario_clue: "nothing at all, for every query, across every workload" - tenant-wide ingestion is off.
questions.misconception: That an empty audit search means no activity happened.

questions.sub_skill: Query Microsoft Purview Audit in Defender XDR
questions.prompt: A user with a Microsoft 365 E3 licence is compromised. You need to establish which email messages the attacker opened. Which audit event do you search for, and what could make it missing?
options: MessageBind - it is only recorded for E5 users

MailItemsAccessed - part of Audit (Standard) mailbox auditing for E3/E5 users; it can be missing if mailbox auditing was turned off or bypassed for the mailbox, or its audited actions were customised before the event existed
SearchQueryInitiated - it lists every message the attacker opened
UserLoggedIn - sign-in records list the messages read in each session
questions.explanation: MailItemsAccessed records mail access by any protocol or client, with bind records listing individual messages. It is part of Audit (Standard) mailbox auditing for E3/E5 users. If mailbox auditing was disabled or bypassed, or the mailbox's audited actions were customised, newer events such as this one may not be recorded.
why_not: MessageBind is only available for users without E5 licences and covers preview-pane access by admins and delegates; MailItemsAccessed is the event built for scoping compromise.
SearchQueryInitiated records what was searched for, not what was opened - and it needs Audit (Premium).
Sign-in events show that and where an account signed in, not which messages were accessed.
questions.scenario_clue: "which email messages the attacker opened" on an E3 user - MailItemsAccessed, Audit (Standard).
questions.misconception: That knowing which emails were read always requires Audit (Premium).
